title: Daily revenue is triple what finance booked
ticket: Finance: the dashboard says yesterday made $36,000; Stripe payouts say $12,000. The numbers diverge more on days with big baskets.

lines: JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id

failing.test: daily_revenue: one paid order of $120 with three items

explanation.cause: Joining to order_items repeats each order once per item, so the order total is summed once per line.
explanation.why: Summing at the grain of the join, item price times quantity, counts each item once. Dividing by three only fixes this one order; the average trick still double counts, and MAX returns one order, not the day's total.

title: Late-evening events land in the wrong day's partition
ticket: Events from our New York customers after 7 pm keep showing up in the next day's table, and yesterday's totals change after midnight UTC.

lines: """The UTC day an event belongs to, as YYYY-MM-DD."""

explanation.cause: fromtimestamp without a tz converts to the server's local zone, so the date depends on where the job runs.
explanation.why: Asking for UTC explicitly makes the partition the event's UTC day everywhere. utcnow() ignores the event's own time entirely, and astimezone() still lands in the local zone.

title: Net revenue: subtract refunds
author: Omar Haddad
description: Finance wants net revenue, so this joins refunds and subtracts them from each order's total.

diff.text: JOIN refunds r ON r.order_id = o.id

explanation.cause: An inner join keeps only orders that have a refund, so every order without one drops out of revenue.
explanation.why: It needs a LEFT JOIN with refunds pre-aggregated per order and COALESCE(..., 0); otherwise net revenue is a small fraction of the real figure, and an order refunded twice still double counts.

title: Index events by user and time for the activity page
author: Elena Ruiz
description: The activity page filters events by user and sorts by time, and it's a sequential scan over 900M rows. Adding the index concurrently so writes keep flowing.

diff.text: -- Runs outside a transaction: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY can't run inside one.
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS events_user_created_idx
-- If it fails, the index is left INVALID: drop it and run this again.

explanation.cause: Nothing wrong: the column order matches the query, and it's built concurrently.
explanation.why: user_id first serves the filter and created_at DESC serves the sort. It runs outside a transaction as CONCURRENTLY requires, and the comment covers the invalid-index case, which is exactly what bit the orders migration.

title: Signups chart shows a third of real signups
ticket: Growth: the signups chart says 41 for yesterday, but 130 accounts were created. Days with a referral campaign look about right.

failing.test: daily_signups: three users on 2026-10-09, one with a referral code

fixes: SUM(CASE WHEN referral_code IS NOT NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS signups,

explanation.cause: COUNT(referral_code) counts only rows where referral_code is not NULL, so users who signed up without a code vanish.
explanation.why: COUNT(*) counts every row in the group. The DISTINCT version and the CASE sum both still count only users with a code.

title: Contacts export still has rows with no email
ticket: Marketing: the CRM import keeps rejecting our nightly export because some rows have no email. clean_contacts is supposed to drop those.

lines: """Contacts we can email: has an address, one row per address."""

output: input: 4 rows, 2 with email=None, 1 with phone=None

explanation.cause: dropna returns a new frame and the result is thrown away, so df still has the rows with no email.
explanation.why: Assigning the result keeps the filtered frame. inplace=False and .copy() still discard it, and dropna() with no subset also drops the valid contact that has no phone.

title: Purchase model is brilliant offline and useless live
ticket: The buys-today model scored 0.97 AUC offline and 0.58 in its first week live. Feature importance says purchases_7d does almost all the work.

lines: -- One row per user per day, zero-filled. The model scores each user at 00:00.
PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY day
ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW

failing.test: purchase_features: user buys once, on 2026-10-09, after a quiet month

fixes: ROWS BETWEEN 7 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
RANGE BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW

explanation.cause: The window ends at CURRENT ROW, so purchases_7d includes the purchases of the very day the label describes.
explanation.why: At 00:00 the model can't know today's purchases, but in training it could, so it learned to read the answer. Ending the frame at 1 PRECEDING uses only the seven finished days; the other frames still include today or look further ahead.

title: Backfill: append the day instead of overwriting the table
author: Tomas Lindqvist
description: Backfilling 2026-10-03 last week emptied the whole mart, because overwrite replaced every partition, not just that day. Switching to append so a backfill only ever writes the day it was asked for.

diff.text: # overwrite wiped every other day's partition, so append just this day

explanation.cause: Append adds the day's rows every time it runs, so a retried or re-run backfill counts that day twice.
explanation.why: The scheduler retries failed tasks, and a task that dies after the write appends again. Keeping overwrite with spark.sql.sources.partitionOverwriteMode set to dynamic replaces only the day's partition, so reruns are safe.

title: Digest audience: NOT IN to NOT EXISTS
author: Grace Okafor
description: Monday's weekly digest went to nobody. unsubscribes.user_id became nullable when we added logged-out unsubscribes, and a single NULL there makes the NOT IN filter match no one. NOT EXISTS skips the NULL rows.

diff.text: WHERE u.id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM unsubscribes)
SELECT 1 FROM unsubscribes s WHERE s.user_id = u.id

explanation.cause: Nothing wrong: NOT EXISTS is the right replacement when the subquery column can be NULL.
explanation.why: x NOT IN (..., NULL) is never true, so one logged-out unsubscribe emptied the audience. NOT EXISTS checks each user's own rows, a NULL user_id never matches, and unsubscribed users are still excluded.
